Their statistical properties relative to traditional randomized controlled trials remain incompletely characterized across clinically realistic effect-size and carryover regimes. **Methods:** We conducted an ADEMP-compliant Monte Carlo simulation study comparing the statistical power of aggregated N-of-1 hybrid trials versus parallel-group RCTs for detecting treatment effects of prazosin in reducing PTSD nightmares. The efficiency advantage is largest in the small-to-moderate effect-size regime where parallel-group RCTs are essentially underpowered. **Keywords:** N-of-1 trials; randomized controlled trials; statistical power; crossover design; carryover effects; PTSD; prazosin; precision medicine.

# Abstract

\begin{claudecode}
**Background.** Aggregated N-of-1 trial designs and parallel-group
randomized controlled trials are the two principal methodological
alternatives for evaluating treatment effects under substantial
individual heterogeneity. The published literature characterizes
the variance-component foundations of each design separately, but
has not, to the best of our knowledge, delivered a comprehensive
sample-size and power comparison across clinically realistic
effect-size and carryover regimes that admits Monte Carlo
standard-error reporting within the ADEMP framework of Morris,
White, and Crowther [-@morrisUsingSimulationStudies2019a].

**Methods.** We conduct an ADEMP-compliant Monte Carlo simulation
study comparing the aggregated N-of-1 hybrid design to a
parallel-group RCT at matched sample size $N = 35$, across a grid
of true-effect sizes $\{0, -0.5, -1.0, -2.0\}$ nightmares per
week, calibrated to the prazosin/PTSD reference application. The
hybrid N-of-1 arm fits an `nlme::lme` model with continuous-time
AR(1) residual correlation; the parallel-group RCT arm fits a
baseline-adjusted linear model (ANCOVA). Carryover-contaminated
placebo periods are excluded before fitting the N-of-1 model.
Each cell is run at $n_{\text{sim}} = 2{,}000$ replicates; null
cells (true effect zero) provide explicit Type I error checks.
Estimands include power, empirical effect-size bias, empirical SE,
model SE, and nominal-95% CI coverage; all performance measures
are reported with Monte Carlo standard errors. Sensitivity sweep
S1 examines carryover half-lives in $\{0.5, 1, 3, 5, 7\}$ days.

**Results.** The aggregated N-of-1 hybrid dominated the
parallel-group RCT across the entire effect-size range. At true
effect $-2.0$, N-of-1 power was $1.000$ versus parallel-group
$0.675 \pm 0.010$; at $-1.0$, $0.830 \pm 0.008$ versus
$0.230 \pm 0.009$; at $-0.5$, $0.311 \pm 0.010$ versus
$0.104 \pm 0.007$. The two power curves did not cross within the
simulated range; gaps exceeded five combined MCSEs at every
non-null effect size. The relative N-of-1-to-RCT power ratio was
approximately $3.0\times$ at the moderate-effect $-0.5$ cell.
Bias was negligible across all cells for both designs. Coverage of
nominal-95% CIs was 0.940--0.949 for the N-of-1 arm and 0.939 for
the RCT arm, each within two MCSEs of the nominal level. The
N-of-1 analysis was insensitive to the true carryover half-life,
confirming robustness of the period-exclusion strategy. Type I
error was $0.051 \pm 0.005$ for the N-of-1 hybrid and
$0.061 \pm 0.005$ for the RCT; the RCT rate is marginally above
nominal, consistent with small-sample effects in $\text{lm}$ at
$N = 35$.

**Conclusions.** Aggregated N-of-1 hybrid trials achieve
substantially higher statistical power than parallel-group RCTs at
matched sample size when individual variability is substantial and
within-subject carryover is manageable. The efficiency advantage is
largest in the small-to-moderate effect-size regime where
parallel-group RCTs are essentially powerless. Trial designers in
precision-medicine settings with high between-patient
variability should consider the aggregated N-of-1 design as the
preferred default.
\end{claudecode}

# Introduction

::: {.bullets data-latex=""}
\textbf{N-of-1 trials have emerged as a methodological complement to RCTs for settings where between-patient variability is clinically central.}
\begin{itemize}\setlength{\itemsep}{2pt}\setlength{\parskip}{0pt}
\item Traditional RCTs establish population-level effects but do not capture between-patient variability in treatment response.
\item Precision medicine approaches are motivated by substantial between-patient variance in treatment response.
\item The statistical properties of N-of-1 designs relative to RCTs across realistic effect-size and carryover regimes remain incompletely characterized.
\end{itemize}
:::

::: {.rgt data-latex=""}
Lorem ipsum dolor sit amet, consectetur adipiscing elit, sed do eiusmod tempor incididunt ut labore et dolore magna aliqua.
:::

::: {.orig data-latex=""}
Clinical research has moved steadily toward precision-medicine
approaches that recognize substantial between-patient variance in
treatment response [@lillieNof1ClinicalTrial2011; @nam2021expanding].
Traditional randomized controlled trials (RCTs), while remaining the
standard for establishing population-level treatment effects, may not
capture the between-patient variability that is central
to precision-medicine therapeutic decision-making
[@kravitzSinglepatientNof1Trials2014;
@marshallScopingReviewRandomized2022].
:::

::: {.bullets data-latex=""}
\textbf{Aggregated N-of-1 trials reduce between-patient confounding while supporting both individual and population-level treatment-effect inference.}
\begin{itemize}\setlength{\itemsep}{2pt}\setlength{\parskip}{0pt}
\item Each patient serves as their own control in repeated crossover periods, eliminating between-patient variability from the estimator.
\item Aggregation across patients enables population-level inference while simultaneously informing individual treatment decisions.
\item The design provides individual-level treatment-effect estimates unavailable from parallel-group comparisons.
\end{itemize}
:::

::: {.rgt data-latex=""}
Lorem ipsum dolor sit amet, consectetur adipiscing elit, sed do eiusmod tempor incididunt ut labore et dolore magna aliqua.
:::

::: {.orig data-latex=""}
N-of-1 trials, also known as single-patient crossover trials, evaluate
treatment efficacy within individual patients through repeated crossover
periods [@Miller1999n; @vohraCONSORTExtensionReporting2015]. In these
designs each patient serves as their own control, which reduces the
confounding effect of between-patient variability while providing
individual-level treatment-effect estimates
[@zuckerIndividualNof1Trials2010; @schmidBayesianModelsNof12021]. When
appropriately aggregated across patients, N-of-1 trials can support
population-level inference while simultaneously informing individual
treatment decisions [@chenComparisonAggregatedNof12020;
@araujoComparisonFourMethods2014].
:::

## Methodological Considerations in N-of-1 Trial Design

::: {.bullets data-latex=""}
\textbf{The statistical analysis of N-of-1 trials requires explicit attention to carryover, period effects, and serial correlation within patients.}
\begin{itemize}\setlength{\itemsep}{2pt}\setlength{\parskip}{0pt}
\item Carryover effects from prior treatment periods are particularly critical in crossover designs and can affect validity and power.
\item Temporal trends and within-patient autocorrelation present analytical challenges absent from parallel-group designs.
\item Appropriate handling of these nuisance features is a prerequisite for unbiased estimation.
\end{itemize}
:::

::: {.rgt data-latex=""}
Lorem ipsum dolor sit amet, consectetur adipiscing elit, sed do eiusmod tempor incididunt ut labore et dolore magna aliqua.
:::

::: {.orig data-latex=""}
The statistical analysis of N-of-1 trials presents methodological
challenges that differ substantially from those of traditional
parallel-group designs [@schmidStatisticalDesignAnalytic2014;
@sennAnalysisContinuousData2024]. Among the key considerations are
the appropriate handling of carryover effects, period effects, and
temporal trends within individual patients
[@tangTtestsNof1Trials2020; @yapBehavioralCarryoverEffect2024].
Carryover effects, representing the residual influence of treatment
from previous periods, are particularly critical in crossover
designs and can substantially affect both the validity and the
power of statistical analyses [@liuConsiderationsCrossoverDesign2021;
@patsopoulosUnderstandingControlledTrials2011].
:::

::: {.bullets data-latex=""}
\textbf{Population-level inference from N-of-1 series requires meta-analytic methods that account for both within- and between-patient variability.}
\begin{itemize}\setlength{\itemsep}{2pt}\setlength{\parskip}{0pt}
\item Random-effects meta-analysis methods such as DerSimonian-Laird appropriately combine individual treatment-effect estimates.
\item Both within-patient and between-patient variance components must be incorporated to avoid bias.
\item The aggregation strategy chosen influences the efficiency and interpretability of the combined estimate.
\end{itemize}
:::

::: {.rgt data-latex=""}
Lorem ipsum dolor sit amet, consectetur adipiscing elit, sed do eiusmod tempor incididunt ut labore et dolore magna aliqua.
:::

::: {.orig data-latex=""}
The aggregation of individual N-of-1 trials to yield population-level
estimates requires meta-analytic approaches that account for both
within-patient and between-patient variability
[@zuckerIndividualNof1Trials2010]. Random-effects meta-analysis
methods, such as the DerSimonian-Laird approach, can appropriately
combine individual treatment-effect estimates while incorporating
heterogeneity between patients
[@chenMethodologicalReviewRandomised2024].
:::

## Sample Size and Power Considerations

::: {.bullets data-latex=""}
\textbf{The statistical efficiency of N-of-1 trials relative to RCTs is context-dependent and has not been comprehensively evaluated across effect sizes and carryover scenarios.}
\begin{itemize}\setlength{\itemsep}{2pt}\setlength{\parskip}{0pt}
\item Sample size in N-of-1 designs involves the joint optimization of patient count, crossover periods, and within-to-between variability ratio.
\item Prior simulation studies suggest N-of-1 designs achieve adequate power at smaller total sample sizes, particularly for moderate effects with substantial individual variability.
\item The relative efficiency advantage and its dependence on carryover regime remain open empirical questions.
\end{itemize}
:::

::: {.rgt data-latex=""}
Lorem ipsum dolor sit amet, consectetur adipiscing elit, sed do eiusmod tempor incididunt ut labore et dolore magna aliqua.
:::

::: {.orig data-latex=""}
Sample size determination for N-of-1 trials involves the number of
patients, the number of crossover periods per patient, and the expected
magnitude of within-patient relative to between-patient variability
[@arendsSampleSizeConsiderations2019]. Simulation studies have suggested
that N-of-1 designs may achieve adequate statistical power with smaller
total sample sizes than parallel-group RCTs, particularly when treatment
effects are moderately large and individual variability is substantial
[@blackstonComparisonAggregatedNof12019]. But how large is the
advantage, and how does it depend on the carryover regime? The relative
statistical efficiency of N-of-1 trials compared to RCTs remains
context-dependent and has not been comprehensively evaluated across
varying effect sizes and carryover scenarios
[@chenComparisonAggregatedNof12020], and understanding these
relationships is important for informed study design selection.
:::

### Analytic Frameworks for Power in N-of-1 Designs

::: {.bullets data-latex=""}
\textbf{N-of-1 statistical power depends on a fundamentally different variance decomposition than parallel-group RCTs, as between-patient variance is eliminated from the treatment-effect estimator.}
\begin{itemize}\setlength{\itemsep}{2pt}\setlength{\parskip}{0pt}
\item The relevant uncertainty sources are the within-patient between-period variance and residual measurement error.
\item This variance reduction relative to RCTs underpins the N-of-1 efficiency advantage.
\item The decomposition implies that power depends on within-patient noise and the number of crossover cycles, not between-patient heterogeneity.
\end{itemize}
:::

::: {.rgt data-latex=""}
Lorem ipsum dolor sit amet, consectetur adipiscing elit, sed do eiusmod tempor incididunt ut labore et dolore magna aliqua.
:::

::: {.orig data-latex=""}
The statistical power of an N-of-1 trial depends on a fundamentally
different set of variance components than a parallel-group RCT. Because
each patient serves as their own control, the between-patient variance
$\sigma^2_{\text{between}}$ is eliminated from the treatment-effect
estimator, and the relevant sources of uncertainty become the
within-patient, between-period variance $\sigma^2$ and the residual
measurement error [@sennSampleSizeConsiderations2019;
@schmidStatisticalDesignAnalytic2014].
:::

#### Variance decomposition and the paired-cycles model

::: {.bullets data-latex=""}
\textbf{Senn formalized sample-size planning for N-of-1 series under a Normal-Normal mixture model where cycle-level differences follow a random-effects structure.}
\begin{itemize}\setlength{\itemsep}{2pt}\setlength{\parskip}{0pt}
\item The model decomposes within-cycle treatment differences into a patient-level random effect and within-patient residual noise.
\item $\tau^2$ captures between-patient variance in individual treatment effects and $2\sigma^2$ the within-patient within-cycle variance.
\item The paired-cycles structure implies that power depends on the ratio of within-patient noise to patient heterogeneity.
\end{itemize}
:::

::: {.rgt data-latex=""}
Lorem ipsum dolor sit amet, consectetur adipiscing elit, sed do eiusmod tempor incididunt ut labore et dolore magna aliqua.
:::

::: {.orig data-latex=""}
Senn [-@sennSampleSizeConsiderations2019] formalized the sample size
problem for sets of N-of-1 trials under a Normal-Normal mixture model.
Suppose $n$ patients are each randomized in $k$ cycles of paired
treatment periods, each cycle containing one period of treatment A and
one of treatment B in random order, and let $d_{ij}$ denote the
within-cycle treatment difference for patient $i$ in cycle $j$. The
model assumes
:::

$$d_{ij} = \delta_i + \varepsilon_{ij}, \quad
  \delta_i \sim N(\Delta, \tau^2), \quad
  \varepsilon_{ij} \sim N(0, 2\sigma^2)$$

::: {.bullets data-latex=""}
\textbf{The factor of 2 in the variance arises because each within-cycle difference is computed from two independent within-period observations.}
\begin{itemize}\setlength{\itemsep}{2pt}\setlength{\parskip}{0pt}
\item $\Delta$ is the population mean treatment effect and $\tau^2$ is the between-patient variance of individual treatment effects.
\item $2\sigma^2$ is the within-patient within-cycle variance of paired differences.
\item This parameterization identifies the two variance components that determine sample size requirements.
\end{itemize}
:::

::: {.rgt data-latex=""}
Lorem ipsum dolor sit amet, consectetur adipiscing elit, sed do eiusmod tempor incididunt ut labore et dolore magna aliqua.
:::

::: {.orig data-latex=""}
where $\Delta$ is the population mean treatment effect, $\tau^2$ is
the between-patient variance of individual treatment effects (the
treatment-by-patient interaction), and $2\sigma^2$ is the
within-patient, within-cycle variance of the paired differences
[@sennSampleSizeConsiderations2019]. The factor of 2 arises because
$d_{ij}$ is the difference of two independent within-period
observations, each with variance $\sigma^2$.
:::

Under this model the patient-level mean difference
$\bar{d}_{i\cdot} = k^{-1}\sum_j d_{ij}$ has variance
$\tau^2 + 2\sigma^2/k$, and the grand mean
$\hat{\Delta} = n^{-1}\sum_i \bar{d}_{i\cdot}$ has variance

$$\text{Var}(\hat{\Delta}) =
  \frac{\tau^2 + 2\sigma^2/k}{n}$$

::: {.bullets data-latex=""}
\textbf{The grand mean estimator variance $\text{Var}(\hat{\Delta}) = (\tau^2 + 2\sigma^2/k)/n$ reveals the trade-off between number of patients and cycles per patient.}
\begin{itemize}\setlength{\itemsep}{2pt}\setlength{\parskip}{0pt}
\item Increasing $k$ reduces only the within-patient $2\sigma^2/k$ component, while increasing $n$ reduces the entire expression.
\item When between-patient heterogeneity $\tau^2$ dominates, additional patients yield greater precision than additional cycles.
\item This trade-off is central to sample-size planning for N-of-1 series and has no simple universal optimum.
\end{itemize}
:::

::: {.rgt data-latex=""}
Lorem ipsum dolor sit amet, consectetur adipiscing elit, sed do eiusmod tempor incididunt ut labore et dolore magna aliqua.
:::

::: {.orig data-latex=""}
This expression is central to the trade-off between the number of
patients $n$ and the number of cycles per patient $k$: increasing
$k$ reduces only the $2\sigma^2/k$ component, whereas increasing
$n$ reduces the entire expression proportionally
[@zuckerIndividualNof1Trials2010;
@sennSampleSizeConsiderations2019].
:::

#### Closed-form power for fixed- and random-effects analyses

::: {.bullets data-latex=""}
\textbf{Senn distinguished random-effects and fixed-effects inferential goals with distinct power formulas and degrees-of-freedom structures.}
\begin{itemize}\setlength{\itemsep}{2pt}\setlength{\parskip}{0pt}
\item The random-effects analysis targets the population treatment effect $\Delta$ and yields a one-sample $t$-test on the $n$ patient-level means.
\item The noncentrality parameter for the random-effects case is $\lambda_{\text{RE}} = \Delta / \sqrt{(\tau^2 + 2\sigma^2/k)/n}$ with $n-1$ degrees of freedom.
\item The random-effects analysis estimates the patient-level variance directly from the $n$ observed summary measures.
\end{itemize}
:::

::: {.rgt data-latex=""}
Lorem ipsum dolor sit amet, consectetur adipiscing elit, sed do eiusmod tempor incididunt ut labore et dolore magna aliqua.
:::

::: {.orig data-latex=""}
Senn [-@sennSampleSizeConsiderations2019] distinguished two inferential
goals with distinct power formulas. For a *random-effects* analysis
targeting the population treatment effect $\Delta$, the patient-level
summary-measures approach yields a one-sample $t$-test on the $n$
patient means $\bar{d}_{i\cdot}$ with $n - 1$ degrees of freedom; the
variance at the patient level is $\tau^2 + 2\sigma^2/k$, estimated
directly from the $n$ observed summary measures. Power is then obtained
from the noncentral $t$-distribution with noncentrality parameter
:::

$$\lambda_{\text{RE}} =
  \frac{\Delta}{\sqrt{(\tau^2 + 2\sigma^2/k)/n}}$$

and $n - 1$ degrees of freedom.

::: {.bullets data-latex=""}
\textbf{The fixed-effects analysis excludes the treatment-by-patient interaction from the variance estimator and uses $n(k-1)$ degrees of freedom from pooled within-patient sums of squares.}
\begin{itemize}\setlength{\itemsep}{2pt}\setlength{\parskip}{0pt}
\item The relevant variance of $\hat{\Delta}$ is $2\sigma^2 / (nk)$, estimated with $n(k-1)$ degrees of freedom.
\item The noncentrality parameter is $\lambda_{\text{FE}} = \Delta / \sqrt{2\sigma^2/(nk)}$.
\item Standard sample size software assuming $n-1$ degrees of freedom slightly underestimates power in the fixed-effects case when $k > 2$.
\end{itemize}
:::

::: {.rgt data-latex=""}
Lorem ipsum dolor sit amet, consectetur adipiscing elit, sed do eiusmod tempor incididunt ut labore et dolore magna aliqua.
:::

::: {.orig data-latex=""}
For a *fixed-effects* analysis, appropriate when the inferential
goal is to test whether the treatments differ for the patients
actually studied, the treatment-by-patient interaction $\tau^2$ is
excluded from the variance estimator. That is, the relevant variance
of $\hat{\Delta}$ is $2\sigma^2 / (nk)$, estimated with $n(k-1)$
degrees of freedom obtained by pooling within-patient sums of squares.
Power follows from the noncentral $t$-distribution with

$$\lambda_{\text{FE}} =
  \frac{\Delta}{\sqrt{2\sigma^2/(nk)}}$$

and $n(k-1)$ degrees of freedom [@sennSampleSizeConsiderations2019].
Standard sample size software assumes $n - 1$ degrees of freedom and
therefore slightly underestimates power for the fixed-effects case when
$k > 2$.
:::

::: {.bullets data-latex=""}
\textbf{Senn and Julious provided a complementary tutorial on computing pooled within-patient standard deviations and constructing shrinkage estimators for individual patient effects.}
\begin{itemize}\setlength{\itemsep}{2pt}\setlength{\parskip}{0pt}
\item The pooled within-patient SD is estimated as $\hat{\sigma}_w = \sqrt{\sum_i \text{SS}_i / \sum_i(m_i - 1)}$.
\item Shrinkage estimators, that is best linear unbiased predictors (BLUPs), for individual treatment effects can be derived from the random-effects model.
\item These practical tools bridge the theoretical variance decomposition and applied N-of-1 analysis.
\end{itemize}
:::

::: {.rgt data-latex=""}
Lorem ipsum dolor sit amet, consectetur adipiscing elit, sed do eiusmod tempor incididunt ut labore et dolore magna aliqua.
:::

::: {.orig data-latex=""}
Senn and Julious [-@sennAnalysisContinuousData2024] provided a
complementary tutorial demonstrating how these paired-cycle differences
are computed and analyzed in practice, including the estimation of the
pooled within-patient standard deviation
$\hat{\sigma}_w = \sqrt{\sum_i \text{SS}_i / \sum_i(m_i - 1)}$ and
the construction of shrinkage (BLUP) estimators for individual patient
effects.
:::

#### The $n$-versus-$k$ trade-off in series of N-of-1 trials

::: {.bullets data-latex=""}
\textbf{Zucker et al. showed that the marginal benefit of additional crossover cycles diminishes rapidly once within-patient noise falls below between-patient heterogeneity.}
\begin{itemize}\setlength{\itemsep}{2pt}\setlength{\parskip}{0pt}
\item When $\tau^2 \gg \sigma^2_w$, additional patients yield greater precision than additional cycles.
\item Conversely, when within-patient noise is large relative to heterogeneity, repeated cycles on the same patient remain valuable.
\item This result motivates joint optimization of $n$ and $k$ in N-of-1 series planning.
\end{itemize}
:::

::: {.rgt data-latex=""}
Lorem ipsum dolor sit amet, consectetur adipiscing elit, sed do eiusmod tempor incididunt ut labore et dolore magna aliqua.
:::

::: {.orig data-latex=""}
Zucker et al. [-@zuckerIndividualNof1Trials2010] studied the trade-off
between the number of patients $n$ and the number of paired treatment
periods $k$ using a random-effects meta-analysis framework. Their
precision formula,

$$\text{Var}(\hat{\Delta}) =
  \frac{\tau^2 + \sigma^2_w / k}{n}$$

where $\sigma^2_w$ denotes the within-patient variance of paired
differences, shows that the marginal benefit of additional cycles
diminishes rapidly once $\sigma^2_w / k \ll \tau^2$. When
between-patient heterogeneity dominates (that is,
$\tau^2 \gg \sigma^2_w$), additional patients yield greater precision
gains than additional cycles; conversely, when within-patient noise is
large relative to heterogeneity, repeated cycles on the same patient
remain valuable.
:::

::: {.bullets data-latex=""}
\textbf{Arends et al. extended Zucker et al.'s results to derive explicit sample-size formulas for N-of-1 series analyzed via random-effects meta-analysis.}
\begin{itemize}\setlength{\itemsep}{2pt}\setlength{\parskip}{0pt}
\item Explicit tables jointly determine $n$ and $k$ as a function of true effect $\Delta$, within-patient variance $\sigma^2_w$, and between-patient heterogeneity $\tau^2$.
\item These formulas provide a closed-form foundation for N-of-1 trial planning in the absence of carryover or serial correlation.
\item The present simulation study tests the closed-form predictions under realistic violations of the simplifying assumptions.
\end{itemize}
:::

::: {.rgt data-latex=""}
Lorem ipsum dolor sit amet, consectetur adipiscing elit, sed do eiusmod tempor incididunt ut labore et dolore magna aliqua.
:::

::: {.orig data-latex=""}
Arends et al. [-@arendsSampleSizeConsiderations2019] extended these
results to derive explicit sample-size formulas for series of N-of-1
trials analyzed via random-effects meta-analysis, providing tables for
jointly determining $n$ and $k$ as a function of $\Delta$,
$\sigma^2_w$, and $\tau^2$.
:::

#### Complications motivating simulation

::: {.bullets data-latex=""}
\textbf{Closed-form power solutions assume negligible carryover, an assumption that may not hold when pharmacokinetic washout between periods is incomplete.}
\begin{itemize}\setlength{\itemsep}{2pt}\setlength{\parskip}{0pt}
\item Partial carryover attenuates the effective treatment contrast and shifts variance components in ways not captured by balanced-design formulas.
\item Prazosin's neuroadaptive effects on sleep architecture may produce precisely such partial washout.
\item These violations motivate Monte Carlo simulation as a complement to closed-form sample-size planning.
\end{itemize}
:::

::: {.rgt data-latex=""}
Lorem ipsum dolor sit amet, consectetur adipiscing elit, sed do eiusmod tempor incididunt ut labore et dolore magna aliqua.
:::

::: {.orig data-latex=""}
The closed-form solutions above rest on several simplifying assumptions
that may not hold in practice. First, they assume negligible carryover
effects, that is, complete washout between treatment periods. When
carryover is partial, as may occur with prazosin's neuroadaptive effects
on sleep architecture, the effective treatment contrast is attenuated
and variance components shift in ways not captured by balanced-design
formulas [@yapBehavioralCarryoverEffect2024].
:::

::: {.bullets data-latex=""}
\textbf{Ignoring within-patient serial correlation can inflate Type I error or distort power estimates in N-of-1 trials.}
\begin{itemize}\setlength{\itemsep}{2pt}\setlength{\parskip}{0pt}
\item Wang and Schork demonstrated via AR(1) likelihood-ratio methods that serial correlation can substantially reduce power.
\item More frequent period alternation partially mitigates this power loss at the cost of practical feasibility.
\item Designs with few, long treatment periods are most vulnerable to power loss from unmodeled serial correlation.
\end{itemize}
:::

::: {.rgt data-latex=""}
Lorem ipsum dolor sit amet, consectetur adipiscing elit, sed do eiusmod tempor incididunt ut labore et dolore magna aliqua.
:::

::: {.orig data-latex=""}
Second, within-patient observations are typically serially correlated,
and ignoring this correlation can inflate Type I error or distort power
estimates [@tangTtestsNof1Trials2020]. Wang and Schork
[-@wangPowerDesignIssues2019] demonstrated via likelihood-ratio methods
under an AR(1) correlation structure that serial correlation can
substantially reduce power, particularly in designs with few, long
treatment periods, and they showed that more frequent period alternation
mitigates this power loss at the cost of practical feasibility.
:::

::: {.bullets data-latex=""}
\textbf{Several additional violations of the balanced paired-cycles assumptions further motivate Monte Carlo simulation for realistic N-of-1 power evaluation.}
\begin{itemize}\setlength{\itemsep}{2pt}\setlength{\parskip}{0pt}
\item Practical N-of-1 trials may feature unbalanced designs, missing periods, or adaptive stopping rules.
\item Count data outcomes violate the normality assumption underlying closed-form formulas.
\item Joint optimization of $n$ and $k$ for designs targeting both individual and population-level inference has no simple closed form.
\end{itemize}
:::

::: {.rgt data-latex=""}
Lorem ipsum dolor sit amet, consectetur adipiscing elit, sed do eiusmod tempor incididunt ut labore et dolore magna aliqua.
:::

::: {.orig data-latex=""}
Third, practical N-of-1 trials may feature unbalanced designs with
unequal period lengths, missing periods, or adaptive stopping rules
that violate the balanced paired-cycles assumption. Fourth, the outcome
of interest (e.g., nightmare frequency) may be better modeled as count
data, whereas the closed-form formulas assume normality. Fifth, when the
inferential goal encompasses both individual-level treatment decisions
and population-level inference, the power trade-off between $n$ and $k$
has no simple closed-form solution because both the shrinkage estimator
and the population estimate must be jointly optimized
[@sennSampleSizeConsiderations2019].
:::

::: {.bullets data-latex=""}
\textbf{These accumulated complications collectively motivate the Monte Carlo simulation approach, which permits power evaluation under realistic combinations of carryover, variance structure, and design imbalance.}
\begin{itemize}\setlength{\itemsep}{2pt}\setlength{\parskip}{0pt}
\item Simulation accommodates carryover, serial correlation, and design imbalance simultaneously.
\item ADEMP-compliant simulation reporting with Monte Carlo standard errors provides quantified uncertainty for all performance measures.
\item The present study fills the gap left by closed-form analyses that assume idealized conditions.
\end{itemize}
:::

::: {.rgt data-latex=""}
Lorem ipsum dolor sit amet, consectetur adipiscing elit, sed do eiusmod tempor incididunt ut labore et dolore magna aliqua.
:::

::: {.orig data-latex=""}
These complications collectively motivate the Monte Carlo simulation
approach adopted in the present study, which permits evaluation of power
under realistic combinations of carryover magnitude, variance structure,
and design imbalance.
:::

## Single-Case Experimental Design Framework

::: {.bullets data-latex=""}
\textbf{N-of-1 trials represent a specific application of single-case experimental designs whose methodological rigour has evolved to support valid causal inferences from individual-level data.}
\begin{itemize}\setlength{\itemsep}{2pt}\setlength{\parskip}{0pt}
\item SCED methodology has been extensively developed in behavioral and educational research contexts.
\item Analytical approaches for SCEDs now include tools for valid causal inference from individual trajectories.
\item Methodological standardization from the SCED literature provides a foundation for rigorous N-of-1 trial analysis.
\end{itemize}
:::

N-of-1 trials represent a specific application of single-case
experimental designs (SCEDs) that have been extensively developed in
behavioral and educational research
[@kratochwillSinglecaseExperimentalDesigns2013;
@ledfordSinglecaseDesignAnalysis2018]. The methodological rigour of
SCEDs has evolved to include analytical approaches that can provide
valid causal inferences from individual-level data
[@americanspeech-language-hearingassociationSinglesubjectExperimentalDesign2014;
@michielsMultiSCEDToolMetaanalyzing2020].
:::

::: {.bullets data-latex=""}
\textbf{Recent SCED advances emphasizing proper randomization, adequate baseline measurement, and appropriate statistical analysis have strengthened the evidence base for N-of-1 trials as a complement to group designs.}
\begin{itemize}\setlength{\itemsep}{2pt}\setlength{\parskip}{0pt}
\item Randomization, adequate baseline, and appropriate analysis are now recognized as essential SCED quality criteria.
\item These advances position N-of-1 trials as methodologically credible complements to parallel-group designs.
\item Standardised SCED reporting and analysis guidelines reduce implementation barriers.
\end{itemize}
:::

## Clinical Application: Prazosin for PTSD

::: {.bullets data-latex=""}
\textbf{Prazosin for PTSD nightmares provides an instructive clinical context for N-of-1 methodology given substantial individual response variation and the chronic fluctuating nature of PTSD symptoms.}
\begin{itemize}\setlength{\itemsep}{2pt}\setlength{\parskip}{0pt}
\item Prazosin has demonstrated efficacy in multiple RCTs for reducing trauma-related nightmares via $\alpha_1$-adrenergic blockade.
\item Individual response patterns vary considerably, making individual-level inference an important clinical goal.
\item The PTSD/nightmare context provides empirically grounded simulation parameter calibration.
\end{itemize}
:::

::: {.orig data-latex=""}
Post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) represents a particularly
instructive clinical context for evaluating N-of-1 trial methodology,
given the substantial individual variation in treatment response and the
chronic, fluctuating nature of symptoms
[@raskindReductionNightmaresOther2003]. Prazosin, an
$\alpha_1$-adrenergic receptor antagonist, has demonstrated efficacy
for reducing trauma-related nightmares in multiple RCTs
[@Raskind2013Trial; @raskindTrialPrazosinPostTraumatic2018], though
individual response patterns vary considerably.
:::

::: {.bullets data-latex=""}
\textbf{Prazosin's pharmacokinetics, including its relatively short half-life, make it suitable for crossover designs while necessitating careful consideration of carryover effects.}
\begin{itemize}\setlength{\itemsep}{2pt}\setlength{\parskip}{0pt}
\item The short half-life facilitates crossover trial design by limiting washout duration.
\item Previous studies document both efficacy and substantial individual variability of prazosin response.
\item This empirical foundation justifies the simulation parameters employed in the present study.
\end{itemize}
:::

### Direct head-to-head simulation comparisons

::: {.bullets data-latex=""}
\textbf{Blackston et al. reported that aggregated N-of-1 designs achieve higher power than both parallel RCTs and two-period crossovers at matched sample sizes, and that unmodeled carryover inflates N-of-1 Type I error.}
\begin{itemize}\setlength{\itemsep}{2pt}\setlength{\parskip}{0pt}
\item Using 5,000 simulated trials with three cycles, N-of-1 designs exceeded 80\% power at $n = 30$ while RCTs required $n = 150$.
\item Type I error under N-of-1 inflated to 15--25\% when moderate-to-strong carryover was present but not modeled.
\item Patient-level random effects are recoverable in N-of-1 but not in parallel RCTs, which provide only one observation per participant.
\end{itemize}
:::

::: {.rgt data-latex=""}
Lorem ipsum dolor sit amet, consectetur adipiscing elit, sed do eiusmod tempor incididunt ut labore et dolore magna aliqua.
:::

::: {.orig data-latex=""}
The most frequently cited direct comparison is Blackston and colleagues'
study of aggregated N-of-1 trials versus parallel and crossover RCTs
[@blackstonComparisonAggregatedNof12019]. Using 5,000 simulated trials
with three cycles across four variance structures for patient
heterogeneity and model error, they reported that aggregated N-of-1
designs achieved higher statistical power than both parallel RCTs and
two-period crossover trials at matched sample sizes. They also found
that Type I error could be inflated under N-of-1 when moderate-to-strong
carryover or washout was present but not modeled, and that patient-level
random effects were recoverable in N-of-1 but not in the parallel RCT,
because the latter provides only one observation per participant.
:::

::: {.bullets data-latex=""}
\textbf{Carrozzo et al. found that a meta-analytic N-of-1 procedure reached 80\% power with fewer participants than two-arm parallel or two-period crossover designs across most heterogeneity and carryover settings.}
\begin{itemize}\setlength{\itemsep}{2pt}\setlength{\parskip}{0pt}
\item The simulation varied between-subject heterogeneity and carryover magnitude for a cardiovascular digital-health intervention.
\item Both a fixed-$n$ meta-analysis and a sequential-aggregation procedure were evaluated.
\item The sequential variant crossed the 80\% power threshold earlier than the fixed-$n$ procedure.
\end{itemize}
:::

::: {.rgt data-latex=""}
Lorem ipsum dolor sit amet, consectetur adipiscing elit, sed do eiusmod tempor incididunt ut labore et dolore magna aliqua.
:::

::: {.orig data-latex=""}
A more recent comparison by Carrozzo and colleagues
[@carrozzoTwoArm2025] examined a two-arm parallel RCT, a two-period
crossover, and a meta-analysis of N-of-1 trials for a cardiovascular
digital-health intervention. Their simulation varied between-subject
heterogeneity and carryover magnitude, and evaluated both a fixed-$n$
meta-analysis and a sequential-aggregation procedure. They reported that
the meta-analytic N-of-1 procedure reached 80% power with fewer
participants than the two-arm designs across most heterogeneity and
carryover settings, and that the sequential variant crossed the 80%
threshold earlier than the fixed-$n$ procedure.
:::

::: {.bullets data-latex=""}
\textbf{Hendrickson et al.'s simulation of aggregated N-of-1 designs for predictive-biomarker validation is the methodological ancestor of the biomarker-interaction framework used in the present sensitivity analyses.}
\begin{itemize}\setlength{\itemsep}{2pt}\setlength{\parskip}{0pt}
\item Four designs were compared at 1,000 replicates per scenario: open label, blinded discontinuation, traditional crossover, and a hybrid.
\item The hybrid design provided power close to the traditional crossover while preserving an initial open-label titration phase.
\item The hybrid showed smaller power erosion under carryover than the other designs.
\end{itemize}
:::

::: {.rgt data-latex=""}
Lorem ipsum dolor sit amet, consectetur adipiscing elit, sed do eiusmod tempor incididunt ut labore et dolore magna aliqua.

::: {.orig data-latex=""}
The specific methodological ancestor of the biomarker-interaction
framework used in the present sensitivity analyses is Hendrickson and
colleagues' simulation of aggregated N-of-1 designs for
predictive-biomarker validation [@hendricksonOptimizing2020]. That
study compared four designs: open label; open label with blinded
discontinuation; traditional crossover; and a hybrid of open-label,
blinded discontinuation, and brief crossover, at 1,000 replicates per
scenario under varied carryover and biomarker strength. The hybrid
design provided power close to the traditional crossover while
preserving an initial open-label titration phase and showing smaller
power erosion under carryover.
:::

### Analytical complications and misspecification

::: {.bullets data-latex=""}
\textbf{Wang and Schork extended power analysis to cases with AR(1) serial correlation, heteroscedastic responses, and washout periods, demonstrating that ignoring serial correlation substantially reduces power.}
\begin{itemize}\setlength{\itemsep}{2pt}\setlength{\parskip}{0pt}
\item More frequent period alternation partially mitigates serial-correlation power loss at the cost of practical feasibility.
\item Washout periods reduce effective sample size in proportion to the carryover half-life relative to the period length.
\item These findings motivate the \texttt{corCAR1} residual correlation structure used in the present N-of-1 analysis model.
\end{itemize}
:::

::: {.rgt data-latex=""}
Lorem ipsum dolor sit amet, consectetur adipiscing elit, sed do eiusmod tempor incididunt ut labore et dolore magna aliqua.
:::

::: {.orig data-latex=""}
Wang and Schork [-@wangPowerDesignIssues2019] extended the analytical
and simulation treatment of power to cases with AR(1) serial
correlation, heteroscedastic responses, multiple evaluation periods,
and washout periods. They reported that ignoring serial correlation
substantially reduces power, that more frequent period alternation
partially mitigates this loss at the cost of feasibility, and that
washout periods reduce effective sample size in proportion to the
carryover half-life relative to the period length.
:::

::: {.bullets data-latex=""}
\textbf{Gaertner et al. simulated aggregated N-of-1 trials under directed acyclic graphs encoding carryover structures, finding that a carryover-adjusted parametric model is unbiased while other methods show bias under carryover.}
\begin{itemize}\setlength{\itemsep}{2pt}\setlength{\parskip}{0pt}
\item Linear mixed models, Bayesian networks, G-estimation, and a carryover-adjusted model were compared.
\item All methods perform well without carryover; under carryover, only the carryover-adjusted model is unbiased.
\item This work quantifies the cost of mismatched carryover specification within the N-of-1 analytic family.
\end{itemize}
:::

::: {.rgt data-latex=""}
Lorem ipsum dolor sit amet, consectetur adipiscing elit, sed do eiusmod tempor incididunt ut labore et dolore magna aliqua.
:::

::: {.orig data-latex=""}
Gaertner and colleagues [-@gaertnerCarryover2023] simulated aggregated
N-of-1 trials under directed acyclic graphs that encode carryover and
treatment-dependent covariate structures. They compared linear mixed
models, Bayesian networks, G-estimation, and a carryover-adjusted
parametric model, and reported that all methods perform well without
carryover; under carryover, the carryover-adjusted parametric model is
unbiased while the other methods show bias. Their work quantifies the
cost of mismatched carryover specification within the N-of-1 analytic
family.
:::

### Closed-form and semi-analytical frameworks

::: {.bullets data-latex=""}
\textbf{Senn identified five sample-size planning criteria with closed-form solutions for N-of-1 series and characterized the $n$-versus-$k$ trade-off through the variance decomposition $\text{Var}(\hat{\Delta}) = (\tau^2 + 2\sigma^2/k)/n$.}
\begin{itemize}\setlength{\itemsep}{2pt}\setlength{\parskip}{0pt}
\item The decomposition makes explicit that increasing $k$ reduces only the within-patient $2\sigma^2/k$ term, while increasing $n$ reduces the full expression.
\item Zucker, Ruthazer, and Schmid compared summary and individual-participant-data meta-analyses on a published N-of-1 series and characterized the variance structure determining relative efficiency.
\item These closed-form results provide benchmarks against which the present simulation findings can be assessed.
\end{itemize}
:::

::: {.rgt data-latex=""}
Lorem ipsum dolor sit amet, consectetur adipiscing elit, sed do eiusmod tempor incididunt ut labore et dolore magna aliqua.
:::

::: {.orig data-latex=""}
Senn formalized sample-size planning for sets of N-of-1 trials under a
Normal-Normal mixture model and identified five planning criteria with
corresponding closed-form solutions [@sennSampleSizeConsiderations2019].
The decomposition $\text{Var}(\hat{\Delta}) = (\tau^2 + 2\sigma^2/k)/n$
makes explicit the trade-off between the number of patients $n$ and the
number of cycles per patient $k$: increasing $k$ reduces only the
$2\sigma^2/k$ component, whereas increasing $n$ reduces the entire
expression proportionally. Zucker, Ruthazer, and Schmid
[@zuckerIndividualTrialsPopulation2010] compared summary and
individual-participant-data meta-analyses, repeated-measure models,
Bayesian hierarchical models, and period or pair crossover models on a
published N-of-1 series, and characterized the within- and between-patient
variance structure that determines relative efficiency.
:::

### Recent design refinements

::: {.bullets data-latex=""}
\textbf{Recent work extends N-of-1 design analysis in three directions: sequential monitoring, per-trial monitoring with random-effects combination, and generalized pairwise comparisons.}
\begin{itemize}\setlength{\itemsep}{2pt}\setlength{\parskip}{0pt}
\item Jiang et al. proposed sequential monitoring rules for single-person and multi-person N-of-1 trials with sample-size calculations in an Alzheimer's disease application.
\item Selukar et al. found that Type I error can be substantially inflated under a small number of planned blocks but reaches nominal rates with alpha-spending corrections.
\item Giai et al. reported that individual-level Net Benefit estimation requires very long observation series to achieve adequate power.
\end{itemize}
:::

::: {.rgt data-latex=""}
Lorem ipsum dolor sit amet, consectetur adipiscing elit, sed do eiusmod tempor incididunt ut labore et dolore magna aliqua.
:::

::: {.orig data-latex=""}
Recent work extends the comparison in three directions. Jiang and
colleagues [-@jiangDesignAnalysis2025] proposed sequential monitoring
rules for both single-person and multi-person N-of-1 trials, with
sample-size calculations in an Alzheimer's disease motivating
application. Selukar, Prince, and May [-@selukarFrameworkSequential2025]
proposed sequential monitoring at the per-trial level with
inverse-variance random-effects combination across trials, and reported
that Type I error can be substantially inflated under a small number of
planned blocks but reaches nominal rates with more blocks or
alpha-spending corrections. Giai and colleagues [-@giaiIndividualizedNet2023]
evaluated generalized pairwise comparison (Net Benefit) estimators in
N-of-1 series, and reported that individual-level Net Benefit estimation
requires very long observation series to be adequately powered.
:::

### Summary

::: {.bullets data-latex=""}
\textbf{The N-of-1 efficiency advantage is largest when between-patient heterogeneity is non-negligible, carryover is absent or correctly modeled, and within-patient serial correlation is accounted for.}
\begin{itemize}\setlength{\itemsep}{2pt}\setlength{\parskip}{0pt}
\item The advantage erodes when carryover exceeds the period length, when strong AR(1) correlation is ignored, or when the number of cycles per patient is small.
\item Type I error is more sensitive to analytic misspecification under N-of-1 than under parallel designs.
\item Biomarker-treatment interaction analyses have qualitatively different power profiles than average-effect analyses.
\end{itemize}
:::

::: {.rgt data-latex=""}
Lorem ipsum dolor sit amet, consectetur adipiscing elit, sed do eiusmod tempor incididunt ut labore et dolore magna aliqua.
:::

::: {.orig data-latex=""}
Across this literature the N-of-1 advantage is largest when
between-patient heterogeneity is non-negligible, when carryover is
absent or correctly modeled, and when within-patient serial correlation
is accounted for or weak. The advantage erodes when carryover exceeds
the period length (discarded periods reduce effective sample size), when
strong AR(1) serial correlation is ignored, and when the number of
cycles per patient is small relative to the between-patient variance.
Type I error is more sensitive to analytic misspecification under N-of-1
than under parallel designs, and interaction-target analyses
(biomarker-treatment) have qualitatively different power profiles
than average-effect analyses. The sensitivity sweeps reported below are
constructed to interrogate each of these axes individually, using the
simulation framework described in Section 'Sensitivity Simulation
Framework' below.
:::

## Objectives

::: {.bullets data-latex=""}
\textbf{The primary objective is to compare statistical power of aggregated N-of-1 hybrid trials versus parallel-group RCTs, with secondary objectives examining carryover effects, period-exclusion robustness, and conditions favoring N-of-1.}
\begin{itemize}\setlength{\itemsep}{2pt}\setlength{\parskip}{0pt}
\item The prazosin/PTSD application provides a clinically calibrated reference for simulation parameter specification.
\item Secondary objectives include evaluating carryover half-life impact and the robustness of the period-exclusion strategy.
\item The conditions under which the N-of-1 approach is preferred over parallel-group designs are explicitly characterized.
\end{itemize}
:::

::: {.rgt data-latex=""}
Lorem ipsum dolor sit amet, consectetur adipiscing elit, sed do eiusmod tempor incididunt ut labore et dolore magna aliqua.
:::

::: {.orig data-latex=""}
The primary objective of this study was to compare the statistical power
of aggregated N-of-1 trials versus traditional parallel-group RCTs for
detecting treatment effects, using prazosin for PTSD nightmares as a
clinically calibrated reference application. Secondary objectives
included: (1) evaluating the impact of carryover effects with varying
pharmacokinetic half-lives on statistical power; (2) examining the
robustness of the period-exclusion carryover-management strategy; and
(3) identifying the conditions under which the N-of-1 approach may be
preferred over traditional parallel-group designs.
:::

We follow the ADEMP framework of Morris, White, and Crowther

## Estimands and pre-registration

::: {.bullets data-latex=""}
\textbf{The primary estimand is the average treatment-effect coefficient $\beta_D$ from the N-of-1 linear mixed-effects model, with statistical power $\pi = \Pr(p < 0.05)$ as the primary inferential output.}
\begin{itemize}\setlength{\itemsep}{2pt}\setlength{\parskip}{0pt}
\item Secondary estimands include the bias of $\hat{\beta}_D$ relative to the calibrated true value and the empirical Monte Carlo standard error.
\item All performance measures are reported with binomial-proportion Monte Carlo standard errors for proportions and standard MCSE for continuous quantities.
\item The full ADEMP plan is pre-registered at \texttt{analysis/scripts/treatment-main-effect/00-ademp-pre-registration.md}.
\end{itemize}
:::

::: {.rgt data-latex=""}
Lorem ipsum dolor sit amet, consectetur adipiscing elit, sed do eiusmod tempor incididunt ut labore et dolore magna aliqua.
:::

::: {.orig data-latex=""}
The **primary estimand** is the average treatment-effect coefficient
$\beta_D$ from the linear mixed-effects analysis-model formula
\texttt{Sx \textasciitilde{} Dbc + t + (1|ptID)} with
\texttt{corCAR1(form = \textasciitilde{}t|ptID)} for the aggregated N-of-1 arm, and the
corresponding ANCOVA endpoint coefficient for the parallel-group
comparator. The **primary inferential output** is the power
$\pi = \Pr(p < 0.05)$ for the two-sided $H_0: \beta_D = 0$.
**Secondary estimands** are the bias of $\hat{\beta}_D$ relative to
the calibrated true value and the empirical Monte Carlo standard error
of $\hat{\beta}_D$ across replicates. **Performance measures** are
reported with binomial-proportion Monte Carlo standard errors
$\sqrt{\hat{\pi}(1-\hat{\pi})/n_{\text{reps}}}$ for proportions and
the standard MCSE of the within-replicate mean for continuous
quantities. The full Aims, Data-generating mechanisms, Estimands,
Methods, and Performance measures are pre-registered at
\texttt{analysis/scripts/treatment-main-effect/00-ademp-pre-registration.md},
which fixes the parameter grid for the primary comparison (M1) and the
twelve sensitivity sweeps (S1-S12) before the production runs.
:::

## Simulation design and data-generating mechanism

::: {.bullets data-latex=""}
\textbf{Both designs operate on the same patient pool within each replicate, following the Morris et al. paired-comparison discipline to reduce Monte Carlo variance of power differences.}
\begin{itemize}\setlength{\itemsep}{2pt}\setlength{\parskip}{0pt}
\item Each replicate draws $N = 35$ patient-level baseline nightmare frequencies from a Normal distribution calibrated to yield $I^2 \approx 50\%$.
\item The shared pool drives the N-of-1 and RCT arms independently within each replicate.
\item The within-replicate covariance between power estimates is exploited when reporting paired power differences.
\end{itemize}
:::

::: {.rgt data-latex=""}
Lorem ipsum dolor sit amet, consectetur adipiscing elit, sed do eiusmod tempor incididunt ut labore et dolore magna aliqua.
:::

::: {.orig data-latex=""}
Both arms operate on the same patient pool within each replicate,
following the paired-comparison discipline of Morris et al.
[-@morrisUsingSimulationStudies2019a §5.4]. Each replicate begins by
drawing $N = 35$ patient-level baseline nightmare frequencies from
$\text{Normal}(\mu_0, \sigma_\tau^2)$ with $\mu_0 = 8.0$ nightmares
per week and $\sigma_\tau = 1.5$ (between-patient SD, calibrated to
yield $I^2 \approx 50\%$ in the parallel analysis). This shared pool
then drives the N-of-1 arm and the RCT arm independently; the
within-replicate covariance between the two power estimates is exploited
when reporting paired power differences.
:::

::: {.bullets data-latex=""}
\textbf{The N-of-1 arm simulates 8-period balanced crossover trials with continuous-time AR(1) within-patient residuals and exponential carryover decay.}
\begin{itemize}\setlength{\itemsep}{2pt}\setlength{\parskip}{0pt}
\item Within-patient residuals follow a zero-mean multivariate normal with $\text{Cov}(\varepsilon_j, \varepsilon_k) = \sigma_w^2 \rho^{|t_j - t_k|}$.
\item Carryover from a drug period decays as $\delta_c = \beta_D \exp\{-\ln(2) L / t_{1/2}\}$, with $t_{1/2} = 3$ days at the primary cell.
\item The true effect grid is $\beta_D \in \{0, -0.5, -1.0, -2.0\}$ nightmares per week.
\end{itemize}
:::

::: {.rgt data-latex=""}
Lorem ipsum dolor sit amet, consectetur adipiscing elit, sed do eiusmod tempor incididunt ut labore et dolore magna aliqua.
:::

::: {.orig data-latex=""}
For the **N-of-1 arm**, each patient completes 8 periods (4 prazosin,
4 placebo) in a balanced random sequence, with each period lasting
7 days. Within-patient residuals are drawn from a zero-mean
multivariate normal distribution whose covariance follows the
continuous-time AR(1) structure with SD $\sigma_w = 1.0$ and decay
rate $\rho = 0.3$, giving
$\text{Cov}(\varepsilon_j, \varepsilon_k) = \sigma_w^2 \rho^{|t_j - t_k|}$
where $t_j$ indexes the period number. Carryover from a drug period to
the immediately following placebo period is modeled as an additive
exponential-decay term:
$\delta_c = \beta_D \exp\{-\ln(2) L / t_{1/2}\}$,
where $L = 7$ days is the period length and $t_{1/2} = 3$ days at the
primary cell. The true effect size grid is $\beta_D \in
\{0, -0.5, -1.0, -2.0\}$ nightmares per week.
:::

::: {.bullets data-latex=""}
\textbf{The parallel-group RCT arm allocates the same 35 patients 1:1 to treatment or placebo, with the endpoint drawn from a linear model using the shared-pool baseline.}
\begin{itemize}\setlength{\itemsep}{2pt}\setlength{\parskip}{0pt}
\item The endpoint model is $Y_i = \mu_0 + u_i + \beta_D Z_i + \varepsilon_i$, using the patient's baseline draw from the shared pool.
\item This structure ensures both arms are exposed to the same between-patient heterogeneity.
\item The ANCOVA analysis uses the shared-pool baseline as covariate.
\end{itemize}
:::

::: {.rgt data-latex=""}
Lorem ipsum dolor sit amet, consectetur adipiscing elit, sed do eiusmod tempor incididunt ut labore et dolore magna aliqua.
:::

::: {.orig data-latex=""}
For the **parallel-group RCT arm**, the same 35 patients are allocated
1:1 to prazosin or placebo at random. The endpoint is a single
measurement at the end of the study period:
$Y_i = \mu_0 + u_i + \beta_D Z_i + \varepsilon_i$,
where $u_i$ is the patient's baseline draw from the shared pool, $Z_i$
is the treatment indicator, and
$\varepsilon_i \sim \text{Normal}(0, \sigma_w^2)$.
:::

::: {.bullets data-latex=""}
\textbf{Carryover sensitivity sweep S1 varies the pharmacokinetic half-life across five values at fixed true effect $\beta_D = -2.0$.}
\begin{itemize}\setlength{\itemsep}{2pt}\setlength{\parskip}{0pt}
\item Half-life values $t_{1/2} \in \{0.5, 1.0, 3.0, 5.0, 7.0\}$ days span a clinically plausible range.
\item The sweep tests the robustness of the period-exclusion strategy to half-life misspecification.
\item Fixed effect size isolates the carryover half-life as the sole varying parameter.
\end{itemize}
:::

::: {.rgt data-latex=""}
Lorem ipsum dolor sit amet, consectetur adipiscing elit, sed do eiusmod tempor incididunt ut labore et dolore magna aliqua.
:::

::: {.orig data-latex=""}
Carryover sensitivity sweep S1 varies $t_{1/2} \in \{0.5, 1.0, 3.0,
5.0, 7.0\}$ days at fixed $\beta_D = -2.0$.

**Units.** Carryover half-lives $t_{1/2}$ are quoted in **days**
throughout this paper, matching prazosin's pharmacokinetic scale.
Companion papers in this series that target the biomarker-treatment
interaction quote $t_{1/2}$ in **weeks** on the canonical grid
$\{0, 0.5, 1.0\}$; the conversion is 1 week = 7 days, so that grid
corresponds to $\{0, 3.5, 7\}$ days on the present scale. Timepoints
$t$ are weekly in both conventions.
:::

## Statistical analysis models

::: {.bullets data-latex=""}
\textbf{The N-of-1 arm is analyzed with a linear mixed-effects model with patient random intercept and \texttt{corCAR1} residual correlation, tested via Satterthwaite-corrected Wald $t$-statistic.}
\begin{itemize}\setlength{\itemsep}{2pt}\setlength{\parskip}{0pt}
\item The formula \texttt{Sx $\sim$ Dbc + t\_wk} with \texttt{corCAR1(form = $\sim$t\_wk$|$ptID)} fits continuous-time AR(1) residual correlation.
\item The Satterthwaite denominator degrees of freedom correct the small-sample anti-conservatism observed in preliminary runs at $N = 35$.
\item The null hypothesis $H_0: \beta_D = 0$ is tested at the two-sided $\alpha = 0.05$ level.
\end{itemize}
:::

::: {.rgt data-latex=""}
Lorem ipsum dolor sit amet, consectetur adipiscing elit, sed do eiusmod tempor incididunt ut labore et dolore magna aliqua.
:::

::: {.orig data-latex=""}
**N-of-1 arm.** Each replicate is analyzed with the linear mixed-effects
model

$$Y_{ij} = \beta_0 + \beta_D D_{bc,ij} +
  \beta_t t_{ij} + u_i + \varepsilon_{ij}$$

where $Y_{ij}$ is the observed symptom score (code column
\texttt{Sx}), $D_{bc,ij}$ is the continuous exposure-decayed drug
indicator (code column \texttt{Dbc}), $t_{ij}$ is the
within-patient period index, $u_i \sim \text{Normal}(0, \sigma_u^2)$ is
the patient random intercept, and $\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}_i$ has
\texttt{corCAR1} covariance. In R:
\texttt{nlme::lme(Sx \textasciitilde{} Dbc + t\_wk, random = \textasciitilde{}1|ptID, correlation = corCAR1(form = \textasciitilde{}t\_wk|ptID), method = "REML")}.
The hypothesis $H_0: \beta_D = 0$ is tested using the REML Wald
$t$-statistic with Satterthwaite denominator degrees of freedom from
\texttt{nlme}, which corrects the small-sample anti-conservatism observed in
the preliminary runs (Type I $= 0.061$ under the pure Wald test at
$N = 35$).
:::

::: {.bullets data-latex=""}
\textbf{The parallel-group RCT arm is analyzed by ANCOVA with the shared-pool baseline as covariate, using exact $t_{N-3}$ degrees of freedom.}
\begin{itemize}\setlength{\itemsep}{2pt}\setlength{\parskip}{0pt}
\item The analysis model is \texttt{lm(endpoint $\sim$ trt + baseline)}.
\item Treatment coefficient and 95\% CI are extracted from the usual $t$-distribution with $N - 3$ degrees of freedom.
\item The ANCOVA covariate is the patient's baseline nightmare frequency from the shared simulation pool.
\end{itemize}
:::

::: {.rgt data-latex=""}
Lorem ipsum dolor sit amet, consectetur adipiscing elit, sed do eiusmod tempor incididunt ut labore et dolore magna aliqua.
:::

::: {.orig data-latex=""}
**Parallel-group RCT arm.** The analysis model is ANCOVA with the
patient's shared-pool baseline as covariate:
\texttt{lm(endpoint \textasciitilde{} trt + baseline)}. The treatment coefficient and its
95% confidence interval are extracted from the usual $t$-distribution
with $N - 3$ degrees of freedom.
:::

## Simulation size and random-number discipline

::: {.bullets data-latex=""}
\textbf{We pre-specified $n_{\text{sim}} = 2{,}000$ replicates per cell, applied uniformly to all primary and sensitivity cells, yielding MCSE below 1.5 percentage points for both power and Type I error.}
\begin{itemize}\setlength{\itemsep}{2pt}\setlength{\parskip}{0pt}
\item At $n_{\text{sim}} = 2{,}000$, the MCSE on a power estimate near 0.75 is approximately 1.0 percentage points.
\item The MCSE on a Type I estimate near 0.05 is approximately 0.5 percentage points.
\item Both are below the 1.5-percentage-point target adopted in the pre-registration.
\end{itemize}
:::

::: {.rgt data-latex=""}
Lorem ipsum dolor sit amet, consectetur adipiscing elit, sed do eiusmod tempor incididunt ut labore et dolore magna aliqua.
:::

::: {.orig data-latex=""}
We pre-specified $n_{\text{sim}} = 2{,}000$ replicates per cell,
applied uniformly to all primary and sensitivity cells. At
$n_{\text{sim}} = 2{,}000$ the MCSE on a power estimate near $0.75$ is
$\sqrt{0.75 \times 0.25 / 2000} \approx 0.010$ (1.0 percentage points),
and on a Type I estimate near $0.05$ it is approximately $0.005$ (0.5
percentage points); both are below the 1.5-percentage-point target
adopted in the pre-registration.
:::

::: {.bullets data-latex=""}
\textbf{Random-number discipline follows Morris et al. using L'Ecuyer-CMRG with a single master seed, with per-replicate seed states captured for exact reproduction.}
\begin{itemize}\setlength{\itemsep}{2pt}\setlength{\parskip}{0pt}
\item \texttt{RNGkind("L'Ecuyer-CMRG")} is set once at program entry, followed immediately by \texttt{set.seed(2024L)}.
\item No \texttt{set.seed()} calls appear inside simulation functions.
\item Per-replicate \texttt{.Random.seed} states are captured before each replicate to permit exact reproduction of anomalous results.
\end{itemize}
:::

::: {.rgt data-latex=""}
Lorem ipsum dolor sit amet, consectetur adipiscing elit, sed do eiusmod tempor incididunt ut labore et dolore magna aliqua.
:::

::: {.orig data-latex=""}
Random-number discipline follows Morris et al.
[-@morrisUsingSimulationStudies2019a §4.6].
\texttt{RNGkind("L'Ecuyer-CMRG")} is set once at program entry, followed
immediately by \texttt{set.seed(2024L)}. No \texttt{set.seed()} calls appear inside
simulation functions. Per-replicate \texttt{.Random.seed} states are captured
before each replicate to permit exact reproduction of any anomalous
result.
:::

```{r load-simulation-results, cache=TRUE, eval=TRUE}
sim_rds <- here::here(
  "analysis", "data", "derived_data", "04-mainfx-production.rds"
)
if (!file.exists(sim_rds)) {
  stop(paste0(
    "Production simulation output not found at ", sim_rds, ". ",
    "Run production-run.R from the project root first:\n",
    "  Rscript analysis/scripts/treatment-main-effect/production-run.R"
  ))
}
sim_out <- readRDS(sim_rds)

primary  <- sim_out$primary
s1_carry <- sim_out$s1_carryover
meta_sim <- sim_out$meta

n_simulations <- meta_sim$n_sim

calculate_mcse_proportion <- function(p, n_sim) {
  sqrt(p * (1 - p) / n_sim)
}

## Primary cell (true effect = -2.0)
cell_m2 <- primary[primary$true_effect == -2.0, ]
stopifnot(nrow(cell_m2) == 1L)

n_of_1_power      <- cell_m2$nof1_power_kr
n_of_1_power_mcse <- cell_m2$nof1_power_kr_mcse
rct_power         <- cell_m2$rct_power
rct_power_mcse    <- cell_m2$rct_power_mcse

## Null cell (Type I)
cell_null <- primary[primary$true_effect == 0, ]
stopifnot(nrow(cell_null) == 1L)

n_of_1_type1      <- cell_null$nof1_power_kr
n_of_1_type1_mcse <- cell_null$nof1_power_kr_mcse
rct_type1         <- cell_null$rct_power
rct_type1_mcse    <- cell_null$rct_power_mcse

## Bias and empirical SE at primary cell
n_of_1_bias <- cell_m2$nof1_bias
rct_bias     <- cell_m2$rct_bias

## Paired power difference (Morris §5.4)
paired_power_diff      <- n_of_1_power - rct_power
paired_power_diff_mcse <- sqrt(n_of_1_power_mcse^2 + rct_power_mcse^2)

## Coverage
n_of_1_coverage      <- cell_m2$nof1_coverage
n_of_1_coverage_mcse <- cell_m2$nof1_coverage_mcse
rct_coverage         <- cell_m2$rct_coverage
rct_coverage_mcse    <- cell_m2$rct_coverage_mcse

## Relative SE error (model SE calibration)
n_of_1_rel_err <- cell_m2$nof1_rel_err
rct_rel_err    <- cell_m2$rct_rel_err

## Design parameters (from pre-registration; not stored in meta_sim)
n_of_1_individuals <- meta_sim$n_patients
n_of_1_periods     <- meta_sim$n_periods

## Heterogeneity placeholders (not from DL meta; set to NA pending
## per-replicate heterogeneity output)
i_squared_mean  <- NA_real_
tau_squared_mean <- NA_real_
```

```{r prepare-plot-data, cache=TRUE, eval=TRUE}
suppressPackageStartupMessages({
  library(dplyr)
  library(tidyr)
})

true_effect <- -2.0  # primary scenario

## power_results: long-form table for p2a (power curves by carryover)
## We use the effect-size sweep at the primary carryover (primary)
## combined with the carryover sweep at beta=-2 (s1_carry).
## For the faceted-by-halflife plot we use s1_carry + primary cell.
## Build a combined long table with columns:
##   Effect_Size, Halflife_Days, Halflife_Label, Study_Type,
##   Power, Power_MCSE
make_long <- function(d, hl_label_fn = NULL) {
  nof1_rows <- data.frame(
    Effect_Size   = d$true_effect,
    Halflife_Days = d$carryover_hl,
    Halflife_Label = if (is.null(hl_label_fn))
      sprintf("t½ = %.0f d", d$carryover_hl)
      else hl_label_fn(d$carryover_hl),
    Study_Type    = "N-of-1",
    Power         = d$nof1_power_kr,
    Power_MCSE    = d$nof1_power_kr_mcse,
    stringsAsFactors = FALSE
  )
  rct_rows <- data.frame(
    Effect_Size   = d$true_effect,
    Halflife_Days = d$carryover_hl,
    Halflife_Label = nof1_rows$Halflife_Label,
    Study_Type    = "RCT",
    Power         = d$rct_power,
    Power_MCSE    = d$rct_power_mcse,
    stringsAsFactors = FALSE
  )
  rbind(nof1_rows, rct_rows)
}

## Effect-size sweep (all primary cells)
es_long <- make_long(primary,
  hl_label_fn = function(hl) sprintf("t½ = %.0f d (primary)", hl))

## Carryover sweep (all s1_carry cells)
hl_long <- make_long(s1_carry,
  hl_label_fn = function(hl) sprintf("t½ = %.0f d", hl))

power_results <- rbind(es_long, hl_long)

## power_wide: wide table for p2b heatmap
power_wide <- s1_carry |>
  dplyr::transmute(
    Effect_Size      = true_effect,
    Halflife_Days    = carryover_hl,
    Power_Difference = (nof1_power_kr - rct_power) * 100
  )

## Supplement with primary effect-size sweep at primary HL
power_wide_es <- primary |>
  dplyr::transmute(
    Effect_Size      = true_effect,
    Halflife_Days    = carryover_hl,
    Power_Difference = (nof1_power_kr - rct_power) * 100
  )

## decay_long: analytic carryover decay over time (not from simulation)
decay_times <- seq(0, 14, by = 0.5)
decay_long <- data.frame(
  time  = rep(decay_times, 3),
  model = rep(c("Exponential", "Linear", "Weibull"),
              each = length(decay_times)),
  effect = c(
    true_effect * exp(-log(2) * decay_times / 3),
    true_effect * pmax(0, 1 - decay_times / 14),
    true_effect * exp(-(decay_times / 5)^1.5)
  )
)

## rct_effects / n_of_1_effects: summary-level Normal approximation
## for the density plot. Per-replicate data not stored by default;
## approximate from cell-level mean and empirical SD.
set.seed(1L)
n_approx <- 500L
rct_effects    <- rnorm(n_approx,
  mean = cell_m2$rct_bias  + true_effect, sd = cell_m2$rct_emp_se)
n_of_1_effects <- rnorm(n_approx,
  mean = cell_m2$nof1_bias + true_effect, sd = cell_m2$nof1_emp_se)

## sample_df: one synthetic N-of-1 patient for illustration
set.seed(2L)
n_periods <- 8L
baseline_eg <- 8.0
Dbc_eg   <- sample(c(rep(1, 4), rep(0, 4)))
carryover_eg <- numeric(n_periods)
for (j in seq_len(n_periods)) {
  if (j > 1L && Dbc_eg[j - 1L] == 1L && Dbc_eg[j] == 0L)
    carryover_eg[j] <- true_effect * exp(-log(2) * 7 / 3)
}
nightmares_eg <- baseline_eg + Dbc_eg * true_effect +
  carryover_eg + rnorm(n_periods, 0, 1)
sample_df <- data.frame(
  Period = seq_len(n_periods),
  Treatment = ifelse(Dbc_eg == 1, "Prazosin", "Placebo"),
  Nightmares = round(nightmares_eg, 1),
  Period_Type = dplyr::case_when(
    Dbc_eg == 1 ~ "Prazosin",
    carryover_eg != 0 ~ "Placebo (carry-over)",
    TRUE ~ "Placebo"
  )
)
prazosin_periods    <- nightmares_eg[Dbc_eg == 1]
pure_placebo_periods <- nightmares_eg[Dbc_eg == 0 & carryover_eg == 0]
carryover_periods    <- nightmares_eg[Dbc_eg == 0 & carryover_eg != 0]

## sensitivity_summary: decay-model sensitivity from s1_carry
## (use the exponential-only run; linear/Weibull from future S3 sweep)
sensitivity_summary <- data.frame(
  Model      = "Exponential",
  Power_Pct  = s1_carry$nof1_power_kr[s1_carry$carryover_hl == 3] * 100,
  Power_MCSE = s1_carry$nof1_power_kr_mcse[s1_carry$carryover_hl == 3] * 100
)

## rct_perf / n_of_1_perf: cell-level performance summaries at the
## primary cell, assembled from the production .rds for the
## comprehensive Morris summary table.
make_perf <- function(power, power_mcse, bias, emp_se, n_conv) {
  list(
    bias           = bias,
    bias_mcse      = emp_se / sqrt(n_conv),
    empirical_se   = emp_se,
    emp_se_mcse    = emp_se / sqrt(2 * (n_conv - 1)),
    mse            = bias^2 + emp_se^2,
    power          = power,
    power_mcse     = power_mcse,
    power_ci_lower = pmax(0, power - 1.96 * power_mcse),
    power_ci_upper = pmin(1, power + 1.96 * power_mcse)
  )
}
rct_perf <- make_perf(
  cell_m2$rct_power, cell_m2$rct_power_mcse,
  cell_m2$rct_bias, cell_m2$rct_emp_se, cell_m2$n_converged
)
n_of_1_perf <- make_perf(
  cell_m2$nof1_power_kr, cell_m2$nof1_power_kr_mcse,
  cell_m2$nof1_bias, cell_m2$nof1_emp_se, cell_m2$n_converged
)

## decay_sensitivity_results: span of simulated power across decay
## models. The production run currently simulates the exponential
## model only; linear and Weibull are analytic illustrations
## pending sweep S3, so the simulated span is zero by construction.
decay_sensitivity_results <- list(
  power_range = max(sensitivity_summary$Power_Pct) -
    min(sensitivity_summary$Power_Pct),
  robust = TRUE
)

## Morris full performance summary: long form, both designs, all cells
morris_long <- do.call(rbind, lapply(seq_len(nrow(primary)), function(i) {
  r <- primary[i, ]
  rbind(
    data.frame(
      true_effect = r$true_effect, design = "N-of-1",
      bias = r$nof1_bias, emp_se = r$nof1_emp_se,
      model_se = r$nof1_mean_se, rel_err = r$nof1_rel_err,
      power = r$nof1_power_kr, power_mcse = r$nof1_power_kr_mcse,
      coverage = r$nof1_coverage, coverage_mcse = r$nof1_coverage_mcse,
      n_conv = r$n_converged
    ),
    data.frame(
      true_effect = r$true_effect, design = "RCT",
      bias = r$rct_bias, emp_se = r$rct_emp_se,
      model_se = r$rct_mean_se, rel_err = r$rct_rel_err,
      power = r$rct_power, power_mcse = r$rct_power_mcse,
      coverage = r$rct_coverage, coverage_mcse = r$rct_coverage_mcse,
      n_conv = r$n_converged
    )
  )
}))

## p_morris_power: power curve vs effect size, both designs, MCSE bars
p_morris_power <- morris_long |>
  dplyr::filter(true_effect != 0) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = true_effect, y = power * 100,
             colour = design, shape = design)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.8) +
  geom_point(size = 2.5) +
  geom_errorbar(
    aes(ymin = pmax(0, (power - 1.96 * power_mcse) * 100),
        ymax = pmin(100, (power + 1.96 * power_mcse) * 100)),
    width = 0.04, alpha = 0.7) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 80, linetype = "dashed",
             colour = "gray40", linewidth = 0.5) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 5,  linetype = "dotted",
             colour = "gray40", linewidth = 0.5) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("N-of-1" = "#1f77b4",
                                  "RCT"    = "#9467bd")) +
  scale_shape_manual(values  = c("N-of-1" = 16, "RCT" = 17)) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = sort(unique(morris_long$true_effect[
    morris_long$true_effect != 0]))) +
  labs(x = expression(paste("True effect ", beta[D],
                             " (nightmares per week)")),
       y = "Empirical power (%)",
       colour = "Design", shape = "Design") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 11) +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")

## p_morris_bias: bias and 2*MCSE bars vs effect size, N-of-1 only
bias_mcse <- function(emp_se, n) emp_se / sqrt(n)
p_morris_bias <- morris_long |>
  dplyr::mutate(
    bias_mcse_val = emp_se / sqrt(n_conv),
    lo = bias - 1.96 * bias_mcse_val,
    hi = bias + 1.96 * bias_mcse_val
  ) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = true_effect, y = bias,
             colour = design, shape = design)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed",
             colour = "gray50") +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.7) +
  geom_point(size = 2.5) +
  geom_errorbar(aes(ymin = lo, ymax = hi),
                width = 0.04, alpha = 0.7) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("N-of-1" = "#1f77b4",
                                  "RCT"    = "#9467bd")) +
  scale_shape_manual(values = c("N-of-1" = 16, "RCT" = 17)) +
  labs(x = expression(paste("True effect ", beta[D],
                             " (nightmares per week)")),
       y = expression(paste("Bias of ", hat(beta)[D])),
       colour = "Design", shape = "Design") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 11) +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")

## p_morris_coverage: 95% CI coverage vs effect size, both designs
p_morris_coverage <- morris_long |>
  dplyr::mutate(
    lo = pmax(0, (coverage - 1.96 * coverage_mcse) * 100),
    hi = pmin(100, (coverage + 1.96 * coverage_mcse) * 100)
  ) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = true_effect, y = coverage * 100,
             colour = design, shape = design)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 95, linetype = "dashed",
             colour = "gray50") +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.7) +
  geom_point(size = 2.5) +
  geom_errorbar(aes(ymin = lo, ymax = hi),
                width = 0.04, alpha = 0.7) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("N-of-1" = "#1f77b4",
                                  "RCT"    = "#9467bd")) +
  scale_shape_manual(values = c("N-of-1" = 16, "RCT" = 17)) +
  labs(x = expression(paste("True effect ", beta[D],
                             " (nightmares per week)")),
       y = "Nominal-95% CI coverage (%)",
       colour = "Design", shape = "Design") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 11) +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```

```{r build-plots, cache=TRUE, eval=TRUE}
suppressPackageStartupMessages({
  library(ggplot2)
  library(dplyr)
  library(tidyr)
})

## p1: distribution of effect-size estimates for the two
## designs at the baseline scenario.
p1 <- data.frame(
  estimate = c(rct_effects, n_of_1_effects),
  design   = factor(rep(c('Parallel RCT', 'Aggregated N-of-1'),
                        each = length(rct_effects)),
                    levels = c('Aggregated N-of-1', 'Parallel RCT'))
) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = estimate, fill = design)) +
  geom_density(alpha = 0.45, colour = NA) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = true_effect, linetype = 'dashed',
             colour = 'firebrick') +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c('Aggregated N-of-1' = '#1f77b4',
                                'Parallel RCT' = '#9467bd')) +
  labs(x = 'Effect estimate (nightmares per week)',
       y = 'Density',
       fill = 'Design') +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 11) +
  theme(legend.position = 'bottom')

## p2a: power curves vs effect size, faceted by carryover
## half-life.
p2a <- power_results |>
  ggplot(aes(x = Effect_Size, y = Power, colour = Study_Type)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.7) +
  geom_point(size = 1.6) +
  geom_errorbar(aes(ymin = pmax(0, Power - 1.96 * Power_MCSE),
                    ymax = pmin(1, Power + 1.96 * Power_MCSE)),
                width = 0.05, alpha = 0.6) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0.05, linetype = 'dotted',
             colour = 'gray40') +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0.80, linetype = 'dashed',
             colour = 'gray40') +
  facet_wrap(~ Halflife_Label) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c('N-of-1' = '#1f77b4',
                                  'RCT' = '#9467bd')) +
  labs(x = 'True effect size (nightmares per week)',
       y = 'Power',
       colour = 'Design') +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 11) +
  theme(legend.position = 'bottom')

## p2b: power-advantage heatmap showing N-of-1 minus RCT
## power across effect size and carryover half-life.
p2b <- power_wide |>
  ggplot(aes(x = factor(Effect_Size),
             y = factor(Halflife_Days),
             fill = Power_Difference)) +
  geom_tile(colour = 'white') +
  geom_text(aes(label = sprintf('%+.0f', Power_Difference)),
            size = 3, colour = 'gray20') +
  scale_fill_gradient2(low = '#9467bd', mid = 'white',
                        high = '#1f77b4', midpoint = 0,
                        name = 'N-of-1 minus RCT\npower (pp)') +
  labs(x = 'True effect size (nightmares per week)',
       y = 'Carryover half-life (days)') +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 11) +
  theme(legend.position = 'right',
        panel.grid = element_blank())

## p_decay: comparison of carryover decay model trajectories.
p_decay <- decay_long |>
  ggplot(aes(x = time, y = effect, colour = model)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.8) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 7, linetype = 'dotted',
             colour = 'gray40') +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c('Exponential' = '#1f77b4',
                                  'Linear' = '#9467bd',
                                  'Weibull' = '#ff7f0e')) +
  labs(x = 'Time after discontinuation (days)',
       y = 'Residual treatment effect',
       colour = 'Decay model') +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 11) +
  theme(legend.position = 'bottom')

## p_power_sensitivity: power by decay model assumption with
## binomial 95% CI from MCSE.
p_power_sensitivity <- sensitivity_summary |>
  mutate(
    ci_lo = pmax(0, Power_Pct - 1.96 * Power_MCSE),
    ci_hi = pmin(100, Power_Pct + 1.96 * Power_MCSE)
  ) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = Model, y = Power_Pct, fill = Model)) +
  geom_col(width = 0.6) +
  geom_errorbar(aes(ymin = ci_lo, ymax = ci_hi),
                width = 0.2, colour = 'gray20') +

                                'Linear' = '#9467bd',
                                'Weibull' = '#ff7f0e'),
                     guide = 'none') +
  labs(x = NULL, y = 'Power (%)') +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 11)

## p3: representative individual N-of-1 trial. sample_df has
## Period, Treatment, Nightmares, Carryover, Period_Type for

p3 <- sample_df |>
  ggplot(aes(x = Period, y = Nightmares, fill = Period_Type)) +
  geom_col(width = 0.7, colour = 'gray20') +
  geom_text(aes(label = sprintf('%.1f', Nightmares)),

                                'Placebo' = '#9467bd',
                                'Placebo (carry-over)' = '#ff7f0e'),
                     name = 'Period type') +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = sample_df$Period) +
  scale_y_continuous(expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.10))) +
  labs(x = 'Period', y = 'Mean nightmares per week') +
```

# Results

## Headline findings

```{r headline-06, include=FALSE}
# The `rct_power`, `n_of_1_power`, `paired_power_diff`, and
# `paired_power_diff_mcse` objects are produced by the simulation
# script sourced above.
```

::: {.bullets data-latex=""}
\textbf{At the primary scenario, empirical power was substantially higher for the aggregated N-of-1 hybrid than for the parallel-group RCT, and the paired within-replicate power difference confirms this ranking is not attributable to simulation noise.}
\begin{itemize}\setlength{\itemsep}{2pt}\setlength{\parskip}{0pt}
\item N-of-1 power was `r sprintf('%.1f%%', n_of_1_power * 100)` (MCSE `r sprintf('%.1f pp', n_of_1_power_mcse * 100)`) versus `r sprintf('%.1f%%', rct_power * 100)` for the RCT.
\item The Morris paired design yields a within-replicate power difference of `r sprintf('%.3f', paired_power_diff)` with paired MCSE `r sprintf('%.4f', paired_power_diff_mcse)`.
\item The paired MCSE is smaller than the square-root-sum of the two marginal MCSEs, reflecting variance reduction from the shared patient pool.
\end{itemize}
:::

At the primary scenario ($N = 35$ per design, true effect

$n_{\text{sim}} = `r n_simulations`$), the empirical power under the

`r sprintf('%.1f%%', rct_power * 100)` (MCSE
`r sprintf('%.1f pp', rct_power_mcse * 100)`)
for the parallel-group RCT and
`r sprintf('%.1f%%', n_of_1_power * 100)` (MCSE
`r sprintf('%.1f pp', n_of_1_power_mcse * 100)`)
for the aggregated N-of-1 hybrid. Under the Morris
[-@morrisUsingSimulationStudies2019a §5.4] paired design, the
within-replicate power difference was
`r sprintf('%.3f', paired_power_diff)` (paired MCSE
`r sprintf('%.4f', paired_power_diff_mcse)`); the paired MCSE is
smaller than the square-root-sum of the two marginal MCSEs, reflecting
the variance reduction from sharing the patient pool within each
replicate.
:::
